jobs.text: When my feelings in the moment pull a decision one way, I want to ask how I will see it in ten minutes, ten months and ten years, so I can separate the decision from my mood.
When I am about to spend real time, money or trust on a venture decision, I want to run a quick check of how it will look later, so I can test my thinking before the commitment is hard to undo.
When I have mapped a system and must choose where to act, I want to rank the places I could push from shallow to deep, so I can find where a small shift changes the whole system.

When I already love the fix I chose, I want to picture the world where it works perfectly and name who loses and which loop pushes back, so I can find its unintended consequences before the system does.

When I face a wicked problem that no single fix can solve, I want to combine several targeted moves at different leverage points, so I can make real progress without pretending to solve the whole thing.
When a problem keeps happening, I want to ask why it happened and then why of each answer, so I can get past the symptom to a cause I can control.
When I have framed a problem as a technical fix, I want to keep asking why it happens, so I can find that the real problem is a different one.
When I am about to commit to a decision, whatever kind of problem I hold, I want to run a quick round of why questions, so I can check that I am not acting on a symptom.

When I face a hard challenge and want a breakthrough and not an increment, I want to frame it, study it, push through the impasse and let it incubate until a new insight comes, so I can build the breakthrough on purpose and not wait for luck.
When a problem has many parts, I want to find the vital few, so I can spend effort where it counts.
When I break a customer's job into its steps, I want to find the few steps that most stop the job from being done well, so I can pick the opportunities worth working on.
When I see a surprising fact that my current story does not explain, I want to infer the best explanation for it, so I can form a hypothesis worth testing.
When a claim sounds confident, I want to trace it back to observation, so I can see where assumption starts.
When I collect needs in a field such as health care, I want to gather many raw observations before I filter them, so I can avoid a confident claim that my data cannot support.
When I interview people about my idea, I want to collect what they actually did and not their opinions about the future, so I can climb toward a claim from real data.
When I see a pattern repeat across many cases, I want to check what the evidence lets me say about it, so I can avoid a claim larger than my data.
When I lead on a wicked problem, I want to test, listen and adjust in steps, so I can improve the solution as I learn.

When something in my venture goes badly wrong and I look for an expert to fix it, I want to sort which parts have a known fix and which parts need the people involved to learn something new, so I can avoid giving a technical fix to an adaptive challenge.
When people bring me a problem that is really theirs to change, I want to place the work back with them, so I can let the people who hold the problem do the learning it needs.
When I pitch to a large institution, I want to test if it can absorb my product, so I can aim at the right buyer.

When I see a design in my domain lock in and need to know how fast it will spread, I want to weigh what each adopter must spend in money and in reorganizing against what it can absorb, so I can predict who adopts first and who lags.
When my research seems to confirm what I already believe, I want to search on purpose for evidence that contradicts it, so I can find the weak points before I commit.
When an AI model agrees with my plan, I want to assign it the opposing role and ask for the strongest case against me, so I can break the loop where my framing and its agreement feed each other.
When my team reviews one hypothesis together, I want one role to hunt for the evidence that would disprove it, so I can hear specific objections and not general complaints.
When I build a product while the needs keep shifting, I want to work in short cycles and show working pieces often, so I can change course before I build too much of the wrong thing.
When I see a group start work without a clear purpose, I want to state the aims, goals and objectives first, so I can keep the thinking pointed at what we want to achieve.
When I am about to build my idea, I want to fake a cheap version first and see if people really use it, so I can know it is the right thing before I build it well.

frameworks.name: Algorithmic Generation of Reverse Salient Solutions

jobs.text: When I search a research field for an opening, I want to find pairs of papers that share a structure but not the same words, so I can spot a cross-domain opportunity that others miss.
When I rely on data or an automated system to decide, I want to audit it for systematic bias, so I can trust its output or correct it.
When my field has no answer to a problem, I want to find a domain that solved a similar problem and transfer its solution, so I can solve it without starting from zero.

When an analogy from another field looks promising, I want to check that the far domain produces its effect through the same causal chain as mine, so I can avoid moving a solution that only shares surface words.
When I look for growth beyond incremental changes, I want a simple map of new offers and new markets, so I can pick where to explore.
When I write the business case for my venture, I want to name the growth direction I chose on the grid, so I can defend that exact claim with evidence in the market attractiveness test.
When I study how a technology spreads, I want to look at the thing, the know-how and the organisation together, so I can see why it holds or fails.
When my analysis rests on beliefs nobody has questioned, I want to list those beliefs and test each one, so I can find the one that could break the whole case.

When I want new opportunities in a market where everyone competes on the same terms, I want to challenge the assumptions about the product or system, so I can find new jobs to be done that others miss.
When a system I study seems stuck, I want to find the assumptions about how its goal must be reached and challenge them, so I can find a point where change is possible.
When I lead without formal authority, I want to act from my real values and with self-awareness, so I can earn trust and keep the team aligned with our purpose.
When I interview customers to test my problem, I want to discount compliments, vague promises, and talk about the future, so I can avoid fooling myself that I am on the right track.

When I ask a room of people at once whether my idea would be useful, I want to treat their nods as social pressure and ask for one dated, costed story, so I can find the real problem behind the polite agreement.
When I hear people say they would buy my product, I want to ask what they actually did the last time instead, so I can learn what I am really competing with.
When my solution ideas stay too safe, I want to allow magical thinking and build stretch solutions that link the ideas from my user inquiries, so I can take a bold option back to users.
When I feel sure my case is special, I want to look up how often similar cases succeed, so I can start my estimate from the real odds and not from my hopes.
When I base my odds on a short stretch of past data, I want to reach back far enough to include the rare events, so I can avoid treating uncertainty as priced risk.
When my innovation could serve many markets, I want to choose one small first market I can win completely, so I can use that foothold to reach the next market.

When I prepare to scale past my first enthusiastic customers, I want to name the one segment I would dominate and check that I have the whole product for it, so I can cross to the cautious buyers who come next.
When I face an undefined problem, I want to question assumptions on purpose, so I can find a better problem.
When I find an industry belief that nobody has changed in years, I want to run Why, What If and How on that belief, so I can turn a habit into an opening.
When I write questions for a customer interview, I want to check what assumptions each question reveals, so I can remove the leading questions before I ask them.
When I suspect my questions carry my own bias, I want to check them against known cognitive biases, so I can ask questions that open the problem instead of confirming my view.
When I prepare questions for customer interviews, I want to rewrite them to ask for specific past behavior, so I can reduce the bias that polite answers bring.
When I see people not act the way my plan assumes, I want to check my assumptions against known decision biases, so I can design for how people really decide.
When I interview customers about my idea, I want to watch for the switch from social norms to market norms, so I can tell polite answers from real behavior.
When I plan for users to leave a product they already use, I want to check the switching costs and user inertia, so I can see if they will really switch.
When an argument for my venture feels convincing, I want to check it against known bias patterns, so I can catch a bias before it drives my decision.
When I want to invent a medical technology, I want to collect and filter real clinical needs before I design anything, so I can build a solution for a need that matters.

When I have a validated medical need and a working concept, I want to plan for what the regulator and the payer must accept, so I can clear the extra gate that a validated problem alone does not pass.
When I have one validated clinical need, I want to generate many concepts for it and screen them with fast think, build, rethink prototypes, so I can let bad ideas fail cheap and early.
When an idea looks good to everyone, I want to spend a set time on only its risks and weak points, so I can find what can go wrong before I commit.
When I have a hypothesis and want to test it, I want to hunt for the evidence that would disprove it before I raise general worries, so I can find the real failure mode and not just sound cautious.
When I have only a few minutes before a decision, I want to write the plan that would make it fail, so I can preview the risks that a full six-hat session would surface.
When I judge ideas or work, I want to remove the names and identifying details first, so I can judge the content and not the person.
When a group debate drifts without an end, I want one voice to manage whose turn it is and call the close, so I can keep order and reach a verdict.

When my hypothesis is still fuzzy and the loudest voice would decide it, I want to look at it through six separate lenses, one at a time, so I can reach a verdict that does not just repeat whoever spoke first.
When I could raise outside money but want to keep control, I want to fund growth from my own resources and early revenue, so I can grow without giving away the venture too early.
When I fund my venture myself, I want to keep it out of the high risk and high uncertainty box, so I can avoid a bet whose total loss I cannot absorb.
When I have won my first niche, I want to use the credibility from it to win the next adjacent niche, one at a time, so I can build enough momentum to reach the mainstream market.
When my first users are packed into one community, I want to widen to the next similar community one step at a time, so I can let my early users pull the mainstream in.
When a project is late and I feel pressure to add people, I want to weigh the cost of coordination and training, so I can avoid slowing it further.
When I have a risky assumption about my customer, I want to build the smallest test, measure what happens and learn from it, so I can decide fast whether to keep going or change course.
When I have filled in my business model canvas, I want to run the first test on the box with the least evidence, so I can check the riskiest part of the model first.

When I have chosen one opportunity on my discovery tree, I want to plug its experiments into a build, measure, learn loop, so I can test solutions for that opportunity and not for all of them at once.

frameworks.name: Building an 'opposite plan' or 'anti-plan' to challenge current plan assumptions.

jobs.text: When I have a well-defined problem to solve, I want to define it, break it apart, prioritize, plan the work, analyze, synthesize and tell the result as a story, so I can reach an answer others will act on without skipping a step.
When I write the statement of the problem I will work on, I want to make its boundaries, success criteria, time frame and needed accuracy clear, so I can start solving the right problem.
When I prepare a business message, I want to check that its logic holds from claim to support, so I can send a message that convinces and does not confuse.
When I design a new business model, I want to lay it out on one visual chart, so I can see value, customers and finances together.
When the guesses on my Lean Canvas have turned into real customers, revenue and costs, I want to move to the fuller Business Model Canvas, so I can map a business that is now mostly proven.
When I prepare to score my business case on market and competitive strength, I want to fill in my business model boxes first, so I can score each domain against real answers.
When I must judge an idea or make a choice, I want to list every factor that bears on it before I decide, so I can avoid a decision that misses something important.

frameworks.name: Can we Win / Competitive Advantage Framework

jobs.text: When I know the problem is real, I want to test if my solution can beat the alternatives people use today, so I can tell if I have an advantage worth building on.

When I prepare to defend a pitch in front of skeptical reviewers, I want to sharpen Can We Win with questions on engineering, durability, monopoly and distribution, so I can answer the objections on resources and market structure before they are asked.
When a problem has many linked causes, I want to draw a causal loop diagram, so I can see the feedback that drives it.
When I keep reacting to one event after another, I want to draw the loop behind the events, so I can work on the structure that keeps producing them.
When I see a whole field of science stuck, I want to draw one loop that shows where money or talent pools, so I can see what keeps the field from moving.
When I face a new situation, I want to ask who can see cause and effect in it, so I can choose between a checklist, an expert, a probe or fast action.
When I have placed a candidate problem on the search gradient, I want to read its causal structure next, so I can know what kind of ground I stand on before I start to dig.
When I need people to act despite obstacles, I want to tell a story of someone who overcame long odds, so I can inspire them to push on.
When everyone in my field accepts the same received wisdom, I want to question it on purpose, so I can find unconventional answers that others miss.

When I see my industry compete on terms that everyone takes for granted, I want to challenge its terms of competition, its strategic logic and its current offerings, so I can find the problems the market does not address.
When I must pick which opportunities in my bank to develop, I want to favor the ones that challenge existing orthodoxies and paradigms, so I can put my effort on the openings with the most impact.
When every player in my market competes on the same things, I want to list those terms and decide which to drop, reduce, raise or create, so I can compete on a basis the others do not see.

When my problem is well defined and I am about to commit to it, I want to name the current terms of competition and choose which piece to break on purpose, so I can create the gap and not only wait to discover it.

When I want to change what a product means to the people who use it, I want to start from the terms everyone competes on and the job and meaning attached to them, so I can imagine a new job or a new meaning for the same thing.
When a situation is in chaos and there is no time to find causes, I want to ask questions that help me act first and stabilize things, so I can stop the bleeding before I analyze.

frameworks.name: CIAs approach to challenging analytical assumptions

jobs.text: When my analysis rests on beliefs I have not checked, I want to list each key assumption and ask what evidence would make it false, so I can catch the one that would break my conclusion.
When I have built a case for my opportunity, I want to search on purpose for evidence that contradicts it, so I can find where it breaks before someone else does.
When cause and effect in my problem are plain, I want to ask verification and fact-finding questions, so I can confirm the known answer and apply it.
When I feel sure a situation is simple because a past success made me comfortable, I want to distrust the fast answer, so I can avoid sliding from clear ground into chaos.
When a group debates and each person defends a side, I want everyone to think in the same mode at the same time, so I can explore the idea together instead of fighting over it.
When I hold a venture hypothesis I am tempted to skip past, I want to write it as one falsifiable what-if and run the six hats on it, so I can name its real assumption before the numeric gates.
When my plan will meet conditions I cannot predict, I want to state the single most important goal in plain words, so I can let the team adapt and still move in the right direction.
When I end a customer conversation with only kind words, I want to ask for a concrete commitment of time, money or effort, so I can tell real validation from politeness.
When I compare my venture to rivals, I want to name my competitive advantage, so I can test if it is different, hard to copy and scalable.
When my market matures and copies of my product appear fast, I want to innovate to find a new competitive advantage, so I can stay ahead of the copiers.
When I validate an opportunity before I commit, I want to ask whether we can win against others who could solve the same problem, so I can drop the opportunities we cannot win.
When I enter a market, I want to map who competes and on what, so I can spot the openings where I could change the game.
When I rank the user needs I could work on, I want to check whether the competitive landscape lets a newcomer in, so I can drop needs I could never enter.
When I prepare to defend my case to investors, I want to state what exists already and why it is inadequate, so I can answer the questions every investor will ask.
When cause and effect in my situation only show after I act, I want to ask exploratory questions and run small probes, so I can learn what works as the pattern appears.
When cause and effect in my problem are real but hidden, I want to ask analytical and comparative questions of the right experts, so I can trace the cause and choose a good practice.
When a wild provocation seems useless, I want to pull out the principle behind it, so I can turn that principle into a practical idea.
When I hear a wild option in a hats session, I want to record it as a provocation and not a commitment, so I can explore it before anyone has to defend it.
When many people add features to one design, I want to keep a single consistent design idea, so I can keep the product simple and coherent.
When my team is in conflict, I want to choose between competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, and accommodating on purpose, so I can resolve the conflict in the way that fits the situation.
When I keep handling conflict the same way, I want to find which conflict modes I use too much and too little, so I can learn to use the ones I avoid.

When I cannot tell what kind of situation I am in because each person gives a different answer, I want to cut the situation into smaller pieces and ask the domain question again for each piece, so I can find the domain of each part before I act.
When I need people to care about my idea, I want to tell a story about people who bridge a gap between them, so I can move my audience to connect and act.
When I feel sure about a judgment, I want to argue the opposite case as strongly as I can, so I can catch the bias before it costs me.
When a constraint makes every solution look impossible, I want to imagine the problem with that limit removed, so I can find ideas that I can then bring back within reach.
When I need to understand how people really work, I want to watch them in their own place while they do it, so I can see needs they would never think to tell me.
When I want to ask a powerful why question about a problem, I want to first understand the situation where it happens, so I can notice what others miss and ask a better question.
When I build a product over many months, I want to talk to a customer every week with my whole team, so I can keep decisions tied to real evidence.
When I hold many unbuilt bets and one outcome to move, I want to sort the bets under that outcome on a tree, so I can see which bets matter before I build any of them.
When I see in my interviews that different groups of customers want different things, I want to narrow the outcome to one group, so I can see which opportunities matter.
When I measure my team by what we ship, I want to replace the output count with an outcome that shows customer value, so I can tell if our work creates value.
When I see my thinking keep falling into the same patterns, I want to add a deliberate disruption or random input, so I can break the pattern and see new options.
When my current product has limited growth, I want to map the capabilities I already own and the jobs they could serve, so I can find credible new uses.
When I have not yet decided what to build, I want to read my capabilities beside the system's bottlenecks and life cycles, so I can sharpen the question before I pick a solution.
When I see my capabilities feed my markets in a fixed chain, I want to lay them out as a funnel from core technologies to platforms to markets, so I can see which markets each core can reach.
When I judge a decision or a plan, I want to ask what would have happened if one key fact were different, so I can see which factors really drive the outcome.
When I want to judge a past decision fairly, I want to ask what someone with only the information available at the time would have advised, so I can separate the decision from hindsight.
When I doubt that I am a creative person, I want to build belief in my ability to change things, so I can act on my ideas.
When I lead a team that holds back its new ideas, I want to build trust, empathy and openness to different views in the group, so I can get the whole team to act on its creativity.
When an old industry starts to fade, I want to see the destruction and the creation as one process, so I can place my opportunity on the creating side.
When I hold a well-defined problem and am about to commit money to it, I want to name what my success would destroy on purpose, so I can plan the break instead of hoping for it.
When I collect opportunities in uncertain ground, I want to picture each prize as a new thing that displaces an old one, so I can tell a real opportunity from a small improvement.
When my team keeps producing the same safe ideas, I want to break the pattern with provocation and random stimuli, so I can reach ideas that ordinary thinking would not.
When I face a messy, open challenge, I want to move through stages that first open many options and then choose among them, so I can reach a new solution that I can act on.
When I need people to accept a new way of thinking, I want to tell a story of someone who solved a problem in a new way, so I can inspire them to try new approaches.
When I define the boundary of a problem, I want to ask who is in, who is out and who decides, so I can see whose interests my definition leaves out.

When I am stuck on a problem in my own field, I want to search other industries for one that already solved the same shape of problem, so I can borrow the solution instead of going deeper into what I already know.

When I find a solution in another industry that seems to fit my problem, I want to check that it works through the same causal chain and not just the same words, so I can avoid transplanting a false match.

When I can name exactly what I want to improve and what gets worse when I do, I want to look up the strategies that resolved that same trade-off across the patent record, so I can start from a pattern already proven in other industries.
When I present an argument to people from another culture, I want to check how they expect reasoning to be ordered, so I can make my case in a form they find convincing.
When I am stuck looking deeper inside my own field, I want to borrow structure from a distant field that already solved a similar problem, so I can find a breakthrough my peers will not look for.

When I want an idea that is new in kind and not just one step further down a known path, I want to bring two fields that never meet into collision, so I can get an intersection idea that no single field would produce.
When I need new territory to search for opportunities, I want to look where two domains collide, so I can open a search space instead of waiting for one to appear.
When the answers in my own field run out, I want to combine ideas from other fields with mine, so I can create solutions that no single field would produce.
When I have built several possible futures, I want to find the patterns that recur across all of them, so I can choose an opportunity that holds up whichever future arrives.
When I advise a firm that cannot know which future will come, I want a strategy that prepares it for every scenario I built, so I can help it act without betting on one forecast.
When I red team the paradigm of my field, I want to keep the opportunities that pay even if the paradigm never breaks, so I can build a portfolio that is worth it in every case.
When I have a startup idea, I want to validate customer segments before building, so I can avoid building something nobody wants.
When I need many ideas to start from in a domain, I want to get out of the building and see what the people there struggle with, so I can collect real present-day problems to work on.
When I need money to start a venture, I want to get customers to pay before or while I build, so I can grow without giving away equity too early.
When I see rival designs in my field rise and settle again and again, I want to find where the field sits in the cycle from era of ferment to dominant design, so I can time my move to the next break.
When I see a new technology appear in my field, I want to tell whether it builds on our skills or makes them obsolete, so I can decide early whether to adopt it or prepare to be replaced.
When I do not know what kind of problem I face, I want to sort it by how clear its cause and effect are, so I can choose the right way to act instead of applying one method to everything.
When I face several situations at once in a crisis, I want to sort each piece into its own domain, so I can act differently on each piece instead of one way on all of them.
When I hear my team give different answers about what kind of situation we are in, I want to cut it into smaller pieces and sort each one, so I can stop the argument and act on each piece.
When I start to explore a new area, I want to first sort how clear cause and effect are and then ask questions that fit that situation, so I can choose the right way to explore.
When I hold many tools and cannot tell which to use first, I want to sort my situation by what kind of cause and effect it has, so I can line the tools up in the right order.
When my team's work is unfinished, I want to show it to each other every day, so I can catch problems early while they are cheap to fix.
When I build the business case for an opportunity that is already well-defined, I want to discount its expected future cash flows to today, so I can compare its value with its cost.

When I face a choice with several uncertain outcomes, I want to draw each option and the futures that can follow, with my best guess of their probabilities, so I can make the choice in a clear and repeatable way.
When I already know the root cause of my problem, I want to map the choices in front of me and what each one costs, so I can choose what to build.
When I see my team disagree about how likely each outcome is, I want to build the tree together with different viewpoints, so I can see more of the possible futures and estimate them better.
When a wicked problem has too many moving parts to see at once, I want to cut it down with two blades instead of trusting the first plausible cause, so I can reach a claim I can defend.
When I line up the points behind my claim, I want to check that each point follows from the one before it, so I can build a deductive chain that holds up and does not mix logics.
When my problem is complex and its pattern shows only after I act, I want to ask exploratory questions and run small probes, so I can learn what the situation is before I commit.
When I start to map the system around a problem, I want to name the one component I study and place it inside each larger system that holds it, so I can see at what level the problem really lives.
When I see my fix to the component I study keep failing, I want to look one level up at the system that holds it, so I can see that the real problem lives at a higher level.
When data is thin and experts disagree, I want to run anonymous rounds with feedback between them, so I can reach a judgment without one loud voice winning.

When I must look far ahead at an un-defined future with little data, I want to add Delphi panels to my scenario planning and long-term trend work, so I can build a portfolio of opportunities for futures that may not happen.
When I have to design a solution and do not know which method to use, I want to pick from a set of systematic design approaches, so I can move from the problem to a solution in a structured way.
When I have a clear problem to solve, I want to follow a user-centered process, so I can build a solution people want.
When my team agrees too fast on a plan, I want someone to argue the opposite side on purpose, so I can find the flaws before the world does.

When I ask an AI model about my plan and it tends to agree with me, I want to assign it the role of my toughest critic, so I can get the strongest reasons my plan could fail and the assumptions each one attacks.
When one dominant assessment rules how my organization reads a situation, I want a standing role whose job is to challenge it, so I can avoid the blindness of a single prevailing view.
When I have a good technology that nobody adopts, I want to test which named actor would say yes tomorrow, so I can pick a first adopter that can actually adopt.

When my first users love the product and I plan to scale, I want to treat their numbers as proof that it can work and not that it will, so I can avoid planning the next stage on buyers who are not like them.
When I choose whom to approach first with a technology that already works, I want to sort possible adopters into bands by their tolerance for risk, so I can tell who moves first and why them.

frameworks.name: Dilemmas in a General Theory of Planning

jobs.text: When every fix I try seems to change the problem, I want to test whether the problem is wicked or tame, so I can stop solving the wrong kind of question.
When I see a social problem that people explain in many ways, I want to list the competing explanations, so I can see that each one points to a different fix before I choose.
When I am asked to call a fix to a public problem right or wrong, I want to judge it as better or worse for each party involved, so I can stop waiting for a true answer that does not exist.
When I plan a venture full of unknowns, I want to list my assumptions and test them one by one, so I can learn before I spend the money.
When a new entrant looks too small to matter, I want to check whether it fits this pattern, so I can tell a real threat or opening from hype.
When I see a technology in my domain improve less and less for each unit of effort, I want to find where it is reaching its physical or market limit, so I can spot the opening for a disruptive entry.

When I wonder whether my own new product is a game changer or only a better version of what exists, I want to ask which job it does for the user, so I can tell if it creates a new game or plays the old one better.
When a new offer enters my market, I want to check step by step whether it can disrupt the leaders, so I can respond to a real threat and ignore the false ones.
When I plan to enter a market that strong leaders hold, I want to test my offer against the disruption questions, so I can enter where the leaders will not fight back.
When no single person on my team has all the answers, I want to let leadership move to whoever has the expertise for the task, so I can use the full strength of the group.
When I need new ideas, I want to generate many first and choose later, so I can avoid judging ideas too early.
When I look for the cause of a failure, I want to open every branch that could hold the cause before I follow the why chain down the likely ones, so I can avoid locking onto the first cause I see.
When I explore uncertain spaces for opportunities, I want to deposit many cheap candidates in a bank first and carry only a few forward, so I can choose my portfolio from a wide field.
When I pick a domain to work in, I want to map its parts and the trends that change it, so I can see where new problems will appear.
When I start to build scenarios for a domain, I want to list every force shaping it that I can find, so I can have a wide range of raw material before I choose the critical uncertainties.
When I notice only the kind of change I already care about, I want to scan my domain category by category, so I can catch the destabilizing change I would otherwise miss.
When I do not know what kind of situation I am in, I want to judge how clear cause and effect are, so I can place it in the right domain and act in the right order.
When I cannot tell which kind of situation I am in at all, I want to break it into parts and place each part in its own domain, so I can treat each part the right way.
When I have placed part of my problem in the complex domain, I want to design one small probe that is safe to fail, so I can learn from it this week without losing more than I can afford.
When a landscape is too wide, I want to pick one domain to work in, so I can focus my effort.
When I start to build a bank of opportunities, I want to pick one domain I know something about, so I can fill the bank with candidates from several tools that point at the same ground.
When I begin to study user needs, I want to choose a domain and a person I can actually reach, so I can observe real behavior and not guess at it.
When I start to explore the future with trends, I want to choose one domain of interest first, so I can find the trends in it and carry one to its absurd end.
When rival designs compete for the same job, I want to tell whether the market is still in ferment or has settled on a standard, so I can choose to fight for the design or compete above it.
When a social habit that people took for granted starts to change, I want to read it as a dominant design that is breaking, so I can find the new needs the change opens up.
When the structure of a whole industry starts to shift, I want to treat that structure as a dominant design in ferment, so I can see the room it opens for new companies.
When my industry has settled on one shape for its product, I want to check how that design got settled and what could crack it, so I can stand where uncertainty returns.

When rival designs still compete for one job and no standard has settled, I want to build the best complement for the architecture gaining ground while I keep my current customers, so I can stand well placed when the design locks.
When the structure of a whole industry starts to break apart, I want to read the old structure as a dominant design that is cracking, so I can see the openings for a new set of companies.
When my technology can serve both a civilian market and a defense market, I want to plan for both buyers and how each adopts, so I can choose a path to market that each buyer can accept.
When I plan to prove a technology first in an extreme and expensive setting, I want to see whether it can spill back into a mass market once proven, so I can plan the path to scale.
When I call my technology dual-use, I want to name a concrete demonstration point and an honest readiness level, so I can show real traction instead of a label.
When I must go from nothing to something I can validate, I want to start from my means and commit only what I can lose, so I can build a venture without a fixed goal.
When I lead a group through a wicked problem with small experiments, I want each experiment to cost no more than we can afford to lose, so I can keep testing without betting the group.
When I have no proof yet and need help to build, I want to recruit people who commit to me before I prove anything, so I can let their commitments shape the venture.
When I sit in high uncertainty with little to lose, I want to start from my means and not a forecast, so I can let the goal change with what I learn.
When I see new technologies appear around my domain, I want to scan and map them, so I can see which ones could open or close an opportunity.
When I lead a team through pressure and conflict, I want to check my self-awareness, self-control, motivation, empathy and social skill, so I can lead the people and not only the tasks.
When a technical decision can affect public health, safety, or welfare, I want to reason through its ethical effects before I act, so I can lead the team to a decision I can defend.
When I see changes happen around me every day, I want to train my alertness to opportunities others overlook, so I can spot and act on them first.
When I want to get better at spotting opportunities over a whole term, I want to add to my bank of opportunities week after week, so I can train my eye to see what others walk past.

When I hold a problem that is still Un-Defined or Ill-Defined, I want to scan the moving market for a gap that is already there instead of inventing one, so I can save the invention work for when the problem is well-defined.

When I am building a new venture under real uncertainty, I want to act, learn from customers, and pivot in short loops, so I can find a business that works instead of following a fixed corporate plan.
When I have several opportunities that all look attractive, I want to evaluate each one against the same criteria, so I can tell which one is worth my time and money.
When the dominant design in my industry starts to break and rival designs compete, I want to read the era of ferment, so I can see which openings exist before a new standard locks in.
When a bet in my growth portfolio may have matured, I want to check whether it has passed its era of ferment and a dominant design has locked in, so I can move it from emerging bet to core business.

When an era of ferment makes me feel sure that my venture will win, I want to treat the ferment as a place to look for opportunities and not as a promise, so I can avoid betting on an outcome nobody can know.
When a business case is built and someone is about to invest in it, I want to check its environmental, social and governance risks, so I can find what is wrong with it before the money is committed.
When I need to show investors my environmental, social, and governance position, I want to find the factors that matter for my kind of business, so I can focus on those and skip the rest.
When I try to see how my product category will change, I want to treat each product as a variant that the market selects or drops, so I can see which designs are likely to survive.
When I keep improving the product I already have, I want to ask whether a new species of technology could replace it, so I can see a break that more improvement will never reach.
When my problem is ill-defined and I do not know where to look, I want to search broadly across many domains, so I can find connections no one in one field would see.
When I see a problem come back after each fix, I want to find the reinforcing loops that feed it and the balancing loops that push back, so I can see why the system keeps doing what it does.
When I look for a small move that can shift a stuck system, I want to add a feedback loop that gives people the information they lack, so I can change behavior without a big intervention.
When I check a venture's finances before a deal, I want to test whether its reported earnings are real and will last, so I can avoid paying for profits that will not repeat.
When I prepare my venture for an investor's or buyer's review, I want to test my own earnings the way their team will, so I can fix weak numbers before they lower my price.
When I start a venture or a project, I want to choose the right people before I choose the direction, so I can adapt when the plan changes.
When a problem could have many causes, I want to sort the possible causes into branches on one diagram, so I can see them all before I choose which to investigate.
When my five whys chase one thread but the problem is too tangled for a single thread, I want to sort its causes on a fishbone, so I can see the other paths back to a cause.
When the branches of my fishbone look thorough, I want to test whether one cause fits two branches, so I can catch the overlap that hides the real cause.
When many organizations try to solve one social problem together, I want to set up a common agenda and the other conditions of collective impact, so I can make their separate efforts add up.

When my days fill with work that does not move the venture, I want to manage my time, focus on contribution, build on strengths, put first things first, and make clear decisions, so I can get the important results done.
When I first describe a problem, I want to answer who, what, when, where and why, so I can have the basic facts before I analyze it.
When I am about to write a well-defined problem statement for an opportunity, I want to gather its story with the five W's first, so I can write a sentence that rests on facts and not on a guess.
When I want my organization to ask better questions, I want a step-by-step way to bring the questioning practice into its routines, so I can make it a habit and not a single workshop.
When people want what I built but still do not use it, I want to check motivation, ability and the prompt at the moment of action, so I can remove the friction that stops the behavior.
When I design a reminder or a call to action, I want to match the prompt type to how much the person already wants to act and can act, so I can avoid the wrong prompt.
When I roll out a new practice that is better for people and they still do not adopt it, I want to ask why a person would actually do the new thing, so I can fix the step that blocks the behavior.
When different forecasts for my market disagree, I want to combine several methods into one estimate, so I can rely on a forecast that is less wrong than any single one.

frameworks.name: Four Actions Framework / Blue Ocean Strategy

jobs.text: When my industry competes on the same factors, I want to ask what to eliminate, reduce, raise, and create, so I can design an offer that moves into uncontested market space.

When I want a new reason for people to buy without a new technology, I want to name the current terms of competition as an incumbent would and sort every factor into eliminate, reduce, raise and create, so I can change the terms instead of the object.
When I look for an opportunity, I want to check all four lenses, so I can find openings from change, needs, habits, and resources.
When the market moves out from under my proven business model, I want to reinvent one part of it on purpose, so I can keep what works and rebuild what no longer pays.

When my working company wants to run a new business model beside the one that pays the bills, I want to audit all four boxes of the current model first, so I can resist the pull back to the model we already know.

frameworks.name: Framework for Question and Answer Clarification

jobs.text: When the question I am asked is vague or badly framed, I want to clarify the question first and then check that my answer fits it, so I can avoid giving a good answer to the wrong question.
When a change arrives, I want to map its chain of consequences, so I can see opportunities that follow from it.
When I am about to spend real time or money on a decision, I want to sketch the first, second and third order effects of the change in five minutes, so I can check my thinking before I commit.
When my industry is in an era of ferment, I want to put the trigger of change at the center and draw its effects outward, so I can see the more disruptive opportunities that sit farther out.
When I take funding for a new or disruptive venture, I want to tell patient capital from impatient capital, so I can avoid money that forces growth before the venture is ready.
When my argument is too tangled to follow in text, I want to draw its claims and links as a map, so I can see where the logic breaks.
When a decision seems to have only the options already on the table, I want to put forward new alternatives as provocations, so I can explore them without anyone having to defend them yet.
When I compete against a much larger player, I want to pick small, fast moves where size does not help them, so I can win ground with fewer resources.
When people doubt they can do something new, I want to lead them through small steps they can succeed at, so I can build their confidence to act on their own.
When I see trends in my domain but no opportunity yet, I want to ask what each change is destroying and who is standing in the wreckage, so I can find a problem someone could build on now.
When I have a trend lead, I want to check it against the frustrations real people live with, so I can drop trends that have no problem attached.
When I find that every industry belief I examine looks solid, I want to reread it after a trend pass, so I can see which belief a trend is about to crack.
When I look for an opportunity through the lens of change, I want to find the trends that are reshaping my domain and ask how to exploit them, so I can move with the change instead of against it.
When I have found the strongest trend in my domain, I want to place its technology on an S-curve, so I can tell whether it still climbs or has locked into a standard.

When I face a trend question that does not warrant a full scan, I want a quick sketch of what the change cascades into and a full PEST pass when the stakes rise, so I can match the effort to the stakes.
When I prepare to pitch my venture, I want to make five checkable claims in a set order, so I can close each door a skeptical investor would otherwise walk through.
When my venture chases too many directions, I want to find where what we can be best at, what drives our economics, and what we care about most overlap, so I can focus on that one thing.

When my team is busy but not delivering, I want to check for a common purpose, specific goals, complementary skills, a shared approach, and mutual accountability, so I can find what keeps us from results.
When people try my product once and do not come back, I want to design a loop of trigger, action, variable reward, and investment, so I can turn first use into a habit.
When my product starts to form habits, I want to ask whether I would use it myself and whether it really improves users' lives, so I can build habits that help people instead of exploiting them.
When I need a hard project moved fast, I want to build a small, driven team around one goal, so I can get intense focus and results.
When I work across several domains, I want to find the links between ideas that are far apart in meaning but share structure, so I can spot surprising cross-domain connections that others miss.
When I must choose which of several ideas to take forward, I want to prefer the ones whose insight is surprising and not obvious, so I can put my effort on ideas that could change the future.
When I design a product or service, I want to involve the people who will use it at every step, so I can make something they truly need.
When a clear problem has too many possible causes to test them all, I want to guess the answer early and test only what could prove the guess wrong, so I can reach the real cause fast.
When I have ranked the bottlenecks that hold a field back, I want to turn each one into a falsifiable hypothesis and test it, so I can let a refuted bottleneck drop and the real one rise to the top.
When I show a concept to users, I want to ask what they like and what they wish were different, so I can get honest feedback that I can act on.

When I see a group discussion on a messy problem go in circles, I want to map the issues, positions, and arguments as a dialogue map, so I can see where we agree, where we differ, and what is still open.

When I find that the current system limits what I can imagine, I want to design the ideal system from scratch and then work back to today, so I can aim for what should exist and not only patch what does.

frameworks.name: IDEO Deep Dive / Structured Brainstorming Techniques

jobs.text: When my team needs new ideas fast, I want to run a structured session that first goes wide and then narrows down, so I can leave with a few strong ideas instead of a pile of notes.
When I have several separate facts that point the same way, I want to group them under one claim they all support, so I can build a conclusion that holds even if one fact is weak.

When I group points at one level of my argument, I want to check that they all follow one logic, either a chain or an inductive group, so I can keep the argument from falling apart under one follow-up question.
When my venture has no revenue yet, I want to track learning milestones with numbers, so I can show real progress without relying on enthusiasm.
When innovation in my organization happens by accident, I want to set up a repeatable way to choose, run and review innovation work, so I can make it happen on purpose.

When I must show whether my innovation work is paying off, I want to pick a balanced set of measures for what goes in, how the work moves and what comes out, so I can judge progress by results and not by activity.
When I run a venture that has no revenue or market share yet, I want to measure progress through learning milestones run in order, so I can prove with numbers that we are learning and not only busy.
When my product looks like every other one, I want to ask what it could mean to people, so I can create value that features cannot copy.
When I see people use an old product for a new reason, I want to notice that its meaning has already moved, so I can find an opportunity that exists before I build anything.
When I have listed and challenged the terms of competition in my domain, I want to ask how the meaning of the product could change, so I can go past a change of features.
When I hold many opportunities at once, I want to sort them into now, new and next, so I can balance safe bets against future ones.

When I split money and people across near and far bets, I want to name a share for each horizon in writing before the fights over headcount start, so I can stop the near-term work from eating the rest.

When my team finds opportunities only through customer interviews, sales talk and watching competitors, I want to check whether we produce any Next and not only Now and New, so I can see when we need tools that look further out.
When I start an innovation effort, I want to first ask what type of problem I face and then pick the tools for that type, so I can follow a path that fits the problem instead of one fixed sequence.
When I run many ideas through an organization, I want to pass each one through set stages with a check between them, so I can stop weak ideas before they cost too much.
When I am stuck in an Ill-Defined problem, I want to dig deep into one domain, so I can find an opening others missed.
When I dig deep into one domain, I want to read it through the four lenses of trends, needs, orthodoxies and resources, so I can find openings from each source of insight.
When I plan the future of a system with the people in it, I want to design together the system we would build from scratch today, so I can plan toward it instead of only fixing today's problems.
When I have an invention to record, I want each part of the disclosure to drive a protection decision, so I can decide if and how broadly to protect it.
When I want to build on a technology, I want to search prior art and check patentability and freedom to operate, so I can know what I can protect and where I could be blocked.
When I am about to launch a product, I want to check it against the active patents that others hold, so I can enter the market without an infringement risk I did not see.
When my team is still choosing between early concepts, I want an early look at freedom to operate, so I can drop a blocked concept before we are attached to it.
When I start a design problem on a technology, I want to search the prior art and the literature, so I can build my technical plan and refine my problem statement on what others already did.

frameworks.name: Is it Real / Problem Validation Framework

jobs.text: When I believe I have found a problem, I want to check with real people that it exists as I describe it, so I can avoid building for a problem nobody has.

When I have a long list of needs from my observations, I want to test each for how often and how badly people hit it and whether they already pay for a workaround, so I can keep only the needs that are real.

When my venture works in a regulated field such as medical devices, I want to show that the problem is real to regulators and payers as well as to users, so I can pass the reviewers who decide if I reach the market.

frameworks.name: Is it Worth It / Value Assessment Framework

jobs.text: When I think I can win an opportunity, I want to check if the return justifies the money and years it will cost against my other options, so I can decide if it is worth doing at all.
When a problem feels too big, I want to split it into questions that can each be answered, so I can find the root cause and test my guesses.

When my logic tree shows the branch that most looks like the answer, I want to state it as a belief I could be wrong about and turn its branches into questions, so I can plan research that holds the belief up or knocks it down.
When a well-defined problem is too big to attack at once, I want to break it into a tree of smaller, non-overlapping sub-problems, so I can find which branch to work on first.

When a question about the future is too wide to explore, I want to build an issue tree to limit the search space before I build scenarios, so I can explore a part of the future I can actually work on.
When I have a hunch about the answer to my problem, I want to list the questions that must be answered to support or disprove it, so I can follow a clear roadmap for my analysis.
When I look for the root cause of a problem, I want to break the problem into branches first, so I can run my why chains down each branch and not just down the first one I see.
When I study a customer, I want to find the progress they are trying to make, so I can design a solution for that job and not for a feature list.
When I cannot tell whether my innovation is sustaining or disruptive, I want to ask which job it does for the user, so I can judge whether it really changes the game.
When I have a flexible product that people can use in many ways, I want to watch the jobs people find for it in their own lives, so I can discover uses I would never have designed for.
When I have found the lagging part of a system, I want to ask what job that part must do to move forward, so I can bring it back into line with the rest of the system.
When people buy what I offer for reasons I cannot explain, I want to find the progress they are trying to make in their situation, so I can design for the job and not the product.
When I cannot tell whether a new product is sustaining or disruptive, I want to look at the job the customer hires it for, so I can judge the change by that job and not by the gadget.
When I have mapped a product life cycle and one stage holds a job that nobody does well, I want to study the progress people seek at that stage, so I can turn that stage into an opportunity.
When I write a value proposition for one buyer, I want to separate what I heard that buyer try to get done from what I only assume, so I can build the offer on the buyer's real job.
When customers tell me what they want, I want to find the progress they are really trying to make in their situation, so I can design for that job and not for their stated preference.
When someone calls a new product disruptive or sustaining, I want to ask which customer job it serves, so I can label the pairing of offer and job and not judge the gadget alone.

When I want to innovate on what a product means without changing the object, I want to name its current job and meaning and then imagine a new job or a new way to see it, so I can find emotional or social needs nobody prices in yet.
When I design a business model, I want to start from the job the customer hires me for, so I can build the model around the progress customers will pay for.

When I have a vague sense of what my users need, I want to write each need as a job statement with a direction of improvement, a measure and the outcome they want, so I can turn the need into a well-defined problem I can test.
When I hear customers say which product they prefer, I want to restate it as the progress they are trying to make, so I can see the opportunity that no current product serves well.

When I use AI to help me research a customer need, I want to keep one provisional job statement beside an evidence ledger and a map of current workarounds, so I can test the need against evidence and not against the AI's answer.
When I suspect others see things about me or my team that I do not, I want to sort what is known to me and known to others, so I can find my blind spots.
When my forecast depends on expert judgment, I want to control for bias with structured methods such as Delphi, so I can trust the forecast more than one person's opinion.
When I see a meeting decide by the loudest or most senior voice, I want experts to answer anonymously in several rounds, so I can keep rank from distorting the answer.

When I am stuck and waiting for an insight, I want to look for a new connection, a contradiction I cannot dismiss, or a fixed assumption to overturn, so I can shift to a better story about my problem.
When I start in a new domain, I want to sort what I know and do not know into the four boxes of the matrix, so I can find my blind spots and tell which kind of problem I really have.

When my team treats a belief as settled fact without checking it, I want to fill the unknown knowns box by asking for the evidence again and again, so I can force hidden assumptions and unwritten expertise onto the page.
When I must decide which Cynefin domain my situation belongs to, I want to read my knowns and unknowns as domain markers, so I can send each part of the situation to the domain where it belongs.
When my thinking keeps running down the same obvious track, I want to jump sideways on purpose with a provocation, so I can reach ideas that step-by-step logic would not give me.
When my product is ready but people do not adopt it, I want to find who is able to say yes first and what saying yes costs them, so I can reach the right adopters in the right order.
When my buyer is an institution and not a single person, I want to ask whether that institution can change shape to adopt what I offer, so I can see the real bottleneck to adoption.
When my business idea is still mostly guesses, I want to put it into nine small boxes on one page, so I can see which guesses to test first.
When my process wastes time and effort, I want to remove every step that adds no value for the customer, so I can deliver more with less.
When I am about to build a venture on beliefs I have not tested, I want to measure progress by what I learn from real customers, so I can change or drop a wrong idea before it costs me the venture.

When my experiments are in and my key metric has not moved, I want to decide on purpose whether to pivot or persevere, so I can change the hypothesis I test next and not stay in a loop the data told me to leave.

When I am about to build a product to test my idea, I want to build only the smallest thing that completes one full build, measure and learn loop, so I can get a real answer with the least time and money.

When I have committed to test my riskiest assumption, I want to build the smallest thing, measure the result, and decide to pivot or persevere on real numbers, so I can learn what is true instead of what I hope.
When growth stalls after launch, I want to change one fundamental hypothesis, such as the customer, the channel or the product, and keep what I learned, so I can pivot without starting over.
When my product works but people do not use it, I want to set in advance the number that shows one behavior has changed, so I can judge my fix on data and not on hope.
When I must pick which assumption in my business model to test first, I want to choose the box with the least evidence behind it, so I can aim my first experiment at the riskiest part.

When I prepare my venture for investment or a deal, I want to review its corporate, IP, contract, litigation and regulatory exposure by risk tier, so I can find the legal problems before an investor does.
When I have signed a term sheet and the no-shop period starts, I want to have my legal and business records ready for the investor's review, so I can close the round inside that short period.
When I lead a venture that has to last beyond me, I want to pair personal humility with strong professional will, so I can build ambition for the organization and not for myself.
When I look for an opportunity, I want to list the skills and assets I already have, not just my products, so I can find a different job those strengths could do somewhere else.
When I see my first market move too slowly for my technology, I want to look for another buyer who needs what it already does, so I can find revenue without a new invention.
When I am a founder with no company assets yet, I want to start from who I am, what I know and whom I know, so I can find what I could build from my own means.
When I want to find overlooked gaps in a product, I want to trace it from raw material to disposal, so I can spot where waste or cost hides.
When I work on a sustainability challenge, I want to measure the environmental impact at each stage of a product's life, so I can find where innovation can cut that impact.
When I have built an argument for my venture, I want to score its structure, relevance, gaps and overlaps, evidence, and clarity, so I can fix the weak links before someone else finds them.
When a problem feels like one tangled lump, I want to group its elements into a tree from big branches to small ones, so I can see the whole territory before I pick a hypothesis to test.
When I have a best guess about a problem's cause or answer, I want to split it into testable claims, so I can test the most important ones first.

When I have no suspected answer yet and the problem has many possible causes, I want to break it forward into every branch that could matter with no overlaps, so I can see the whole territory before I pick a branch to test.
When I already know what is broken and must choose what to build, I want to map the choices in front of me and what each one costs, so I can pick a fix on purpose.
When I look for opportunities, I want to start from broad shifts in society, so I can find openings that grow with the trend.
When I have picked a domain and have no problem yet, I want to ask what is changing in it and who is losing because of the change, so I can find what someone could build on that loss now.
When my field research only shows what users struggle with today, I want to step back to the long-range shifts in the world, so I can find bigger ideas that present complaints hide.
When I explore an ill-defined domain, I want to list the political, economic, social, technological, and other macro trends that act on it, so I can find the changes that create opportunities.
When I compare the opportunities in my bank, I want to favor those that take advantage of current macro trends, so I can put my effort on openings that grow with the trend.
When I want to start a venture but have no product passion yet, I want to begin from a macro trend I see growing early, so I can evaluate opportunities before competitors notice the trend.

When I look for where new business opportunities will come from, I want to scan my domain for changes in technology, in political and regulatory rules, in social and demographic factors and in industry structure, so I can find the problems and openings those changes create.
When I have picked a domain that is changing, I want to trace what each big change destroys and which dominant designs it breaks, so I can name the next big problems worth solving.
When I compare technology changes as sources of opportunity, I want to weigh how large each change is, so I can favor the changes that open the most new uses.
When I look for an opening in an existing market, I want to look for the gaps that alert people notice and others miss, so I can find an opportunity that is already there.
When I keep scanning for one more signal after my problem is already well-defined, I want to notice that I am stuck in discovery, so I can stop scanning and start building.
When an innovation project has many parallel tasks and deadlines, I want one shared timeline, so I can see what is due and keep the work moving.
When I must split resources between today's business and future bets, I want to sort my work into the core, the emerging and the transformational, so I can fund each at the right level of risk.
When I see a long-shot project judged by the core business's quarterly numbers, I want to give each horizon its own metrics and tolerance for failure, so I can stop the core from killing future bets.
When I plan bets that may not pay off for years, I want to fund them as options and not as plans, so I can pay for learning without demanding certainty.
When I split a problem into parts, I want to check for overlaps and gaps, so I can be sure I did not double count or miss a cause.

When I list the routes to a scientific or technical goal past a bottleneck, I want to hold the list to no overlaps and no gaps, including routes far from current work, so I can avoid missing the path nobody is trying.
When I group the reasons under my main answer, I want to check that the groups do not overlap and leave nothing material out, so I can make my support hold up when a skeptical reader checks it.
When I break a problem into parts, I want each part to be separate and the set to be complete, so I can see that nothing is missing or counted twice before I choose what to test.

When I group the reasons under the main point of an argument, I want each group to be separate and the set to be complete, so I can give a skeptical reader support they can follow and not overlapping guesses.
When I list the routes to an ambitious technical goal, I want the routes to be separate and to cover every option, so I can find paths far from what anyone is trying now.

When I group cases or candidate explanations from an investigation, I want to check that no case fits two groups and no important case fits none, so I can expose overlap and omission in my classification.
When I study the long-term future of a domain, I want to find the large, slow trends that change whole societies, so I can see the problems and opportunities they will create.
When I face a decision with long-term effects, I want to consult my past and future self, so I can choose with the consequences in view.
When I must decide under deadline pressure and my mood is strong, I want to ask how the choice will look in 10 minutes, 10 months and 10 years, so I can separate the decision from how it feels now.
When I am about to launch, hire or sign a deal, I want to assume it has already failed and write the history of that failure, so I can find what would break first while I can still change it.
When I choose a forecast for a scenario axis, I want to match the method to my horizon and data, so I can avoid guessing with extra steps.

When I answer whether an opportunity is real, winnable and worth it from a forecast, I want to know how the forecast was made and how far to trust it, so I can weigh each answer by the strength of what feeds it.
When my thoughts about a problem are a tangled pile, I want to put them on one page around a central idea, so I can see the parts and how they connect.

When I have finished primary and secondary research on the opportunity I chose, I want to put everything I know about the space on one map, so I can define the problem by what the solution must deliver.
When I am ready to break my problem into its parts, I want to use my mind map as the raw material for an issue tree, so I can structure the parts without losing what I found.

When I have gathered research on an opportunity and my notes are tangled, I want to put the problem at the center of one map and hang what I know on a few main branches, so I can see the connections and themes before I structure the problem.

When I observe people at work in the field, I want to record what I see on a mind map under plain headings such as people, products, process and place, so I can capture observations I would lose in a list.
When I start research on a chosen opportunity, I want to make a mind map of everything I know about the space, so I can define the problem by what a solution must deliver.
When I have a solution idea, I want to build the smallest version that tests my riskiest assumption, so I can learn what the market wants before I invest more.
When I need a starting point for measuring my venture's progress, I want to run my MVP with real customers and write down the actual numbers, so I can tune the business from a true baseline.

When I am not sure whether my biggest doubt is the technology, the user experience or the demand, I want to place my work on the proof of concept, prototype and MVP ladder, so I can build an MVP only when demand is the open question.
When I must convince a busy reader, I want to state my answer first and group the reasons under it, so I can make every sentence prove the point.
When I must pitch my venture out loud to investors, I want to put my answer first and group my evidence under it, so I can keep listeners from building their own guess while I talk.
When my investigation across cases has reached a conclusion, I want to state the conclusion first and support it with grouped reasons, so I can hand others a finding they can check.
When I face a large societal challenge, I want to break it into one bold, concrete mission that many actors can work toward, so I can aim innovation at the problem and not at one industry.
When I need to know if my venture has a real business case, I want to test it on several dimensions with evidence, so I can see where it is weak.

When my opportunity has moved past exploring and its goal is defined enough to plan backward from, I want to switch from effectual moves to the Mullins grid, so I can build a causal business case that I can execute.
When my venture serves both civilian and defense users, I want to size the market attractiveness of each side on its own clock, so I can see whether the institution I need first will decide in time.

frameworks.name: Mullins Model for the Business Case / Mullins Model Validation

jobs.text: When I need to know if my opportunity can become a real business, I want to test it across Mullins' seven domains, from market and industry to team, so I can find the red light before I commit years to it.
When I am about to score my venture on Mullins' domains, I want to fill in my business model canvas first, so I can score market and advantage against real boxes and not guesses.
When I finish the Mullins work, I want to state one top-line verdict for the whole venture, so I can say plainly whether it deserves to be built.
When I build a business case for a medical device, I want the Mullins questions to satisfy a regulator and an insurer as well as the market, so I can plan for the buyers who decide in medtech.

When one tool shows only part of my opportunity, I want to chain several tools in a planned order, such as jobs to be done, reverse salient and the S-curve, so I can see the whole opportunity and not one piece of it.
When I explore an ill-defined problem, I want to scan the short-horizon trends in consumers, technology, and new competitors, so I can find what is changing now that opens an opportunity.
When I must decide which markets to enter next, I want to read near-term trends and emerging technologies, so I can answer what the next opportunity is.
When I have built an argument, I want to score its structure, relevance, grouping, evidence and clarity, so I can find the weakest part before someone else does.
When I explore a domain, I want to place it inside the larger systems around it, so I can see which level holds the opportunity.
When I face a systems problem that resists my fixes, I want to find which level of the hierarchy holds my intervention point, so I can push where the system can actually move.
When I imagine a disruption to a system, I want to trace its effects at every level from the people to the policy, so I can see the new problems each level would face.
When good ideas stay stuck with a few people at the top, I want to give everyone in the company one day to suggest how to improve the work, so I can collect ideas from the whole organization.
When I plan an innovation portfolio, I want to sort ideas by Now, New and Next, so I can balance near and far bets.

When I have sorted my team's initiatives into Now, New and Next, I want to place each one on the uncertainty versus risk grid, so I can check that my Next bets take on market or technology uncertainty without heavy risk.
When I see my portfolio hold plenty of Now and New but little Next, I want to ask where Next ideas actually come from, so I can source them through a process and not wait for inspiration.
When a rival or a fast market keeps getting ahead of me, I want to time and shorten my own observe, orient, decide, and act cycle, so I can act inside their cycle instead of behind it.
When I see that my team's decisions wait on approval several layers up, I want to give the authority to the people who see the signal, so I can shorten the loop without new tools.
When I and my team read the same event in different ways, I want to examine how our past experience filters what we notice, so I can act on what is there and not on what we assumed.
When my team cannot build every idea alone, I want to bring ideas in from outside and send unused ideas out, so I can move faster than my own lab allows.
When I want users to help shape my next products, I want to open a program where users design new products, so I can draw on ideas from outside my team.
When I explore un-defined and ill-defined spaces, I want to keep every promising opportunity in one shared bank, so I can pick the best ones to develop.
When I hear someone else's idea in a review that I like, I want to write it down in my own book, so I can draw on it later because every idea in the bank belongs to everyone.
When I see events and trends that seem unrelated, I want to look for the pattern that connects them, so I can spot an opportunity that others walk past.
When I study a body of research or a technology field, I want to look for the holes in the pattern as well as the whole, so I can find the missing piece where an opportunity sits.
When I see many unrelated changes in technology, markets, and policy, I want to connect them into a pattern, so I can see an opportunity that the separate changes hide.
When I know the outcomes customers want but not which ones matter most, I want to score each outcome on importance and current satisfaction, so I can find the underserved outcomes worth building for.
When I write down what a customer needs from a step, I want to phrase it as an outcome with a direction of improvement and a unit of measure, so I can score how well that outcome is satisfied today.
When I find a good opportunity, I want to check how long the window stays open before the uncertainty falls and better funded players arrive, so I can act while a small team can still win.
When I see the old standard in my field cracking and no new design has won yet, I want to treat that stretch as the window to enter, so I can move while incumbents cannot buy their way to safety.
When I have a technology that already works and I plan to move first, I want to ask how long the first mover advantage will last, so I can plan for the moment the window closes.

When my plan rests on assumptions I have not checked, I want to write the plan that follows if those assumptions are inverted and compare it with mine, so I can see which assumptions carry the most risk.
When I get a result, good or bad, I want to sort how much came from my decision and how much from luck, so I can learn the right lesson from it.
When I hear people call a forecast wrong only because the unlikely outcome happened, I want to ask whether the forecast was sound when it was made, so I can avoid judging the decision by its result.
When I know the job my customers hire a product for, I want to list their desired outcomes and score each for importance and satisfaction, so I can find the outcomes that are underserved.
When my customers seem to want different things, I want to group them by which outcomes they rate as unmet, so I can find hidden segments to serve first.
When I plan customer research that must stay useful for years, I want to capture a complete set of desired outcome statements, so I can reuse them while the solutions that serve them change.
When I study a process or a user's day, I want to mark the steps where people struggle against how well each step works, so I can find the pain worth solving.
When I test whether a pain is real, I want to score it by what people did about it, such as time, money or a workaround, so I can trust actions over kind words.

When I spend hours inside a clinical setting, I want to record what goes wrong and screen it by how many people it hits and how bad the workaround is, so I can narrow many observations to the needs worth work.
When I look across scenarios or markets, I want to spot what repeats or breaks down, so I can imagine a new solution.
When I look at a crowded market map, I want to see the whole and also the holes in it, so I can spot what is missing that nobody offers yet.
