When I explore a domain, I want to scan the political, economic, social and technological changes around it, so I can find the outside forces that create new problems and openings.
When I see one trend grow fast, I want to ask what it implies politically, economically, socially and technologically, so I can find the consequences that are not obvious.
When I face a pile of trends in a domain, I want to sort them into political, economic, social and technological forces, so I can see where several forces shake the domain at once.
When one trend is growing fast, I want to ask what it changes politically, economically, socially and technologically, so I can see what it destroys and what new opportunities it opens.
When I start a scenario analysis for a domain, I want to gather background on its political, economic, social and technological changes, so I can pick the driving forces for my scenarios.
When my tests show the current hypothesis fails, I want to change one core element and keep what I learned, so I can keep moving without starting over.
When I set up a weekly experiment, I want to fix the hypothesis, the metric and the threshold before I see the data, so I can pivot on the number and not on hope.
When I change one thing to fix a stalled behavior, I want to write down the number that proves the fix worked before I ship it, so I can read the result without bias.
When I design a product, I want to build a base others can build on, so I can let many solutions grow.
When I scale a platform and nobody joins until someone else is already there, I want to find who has to show up first, so I can make the next person bother to join.
When my business model must bring together two groups who need each other, I want to treat my job as lowering the cost of their interaction, so I can make network effects my central strategic lever.

When I hold more opportunities in my bank than I can pursue, I want to choose a small set of the best ones to carry forward as well-defined problems, so I can spread my bets and not stake everything on one guess.
When I plan growth for a company that already has a core business, I want to split my innovation into now, new and next, so I can keep today's business strong while I seed the future.

When I have imagined how a dominant product could disappear, I want to build a portfolio of opportunities across those alternative futures, so I can hold some bets that stay viable even if the shift does not come.
When I am about to commit to a launch, a hire, or a deal, I want to imagine it has already failed and write how it broke, so I can fix the cause before it happens.
When I have a problem that is still vague, I want to move it step by step from an open area to a bounded, testable statement, so I can work on a problem I can actually solve.

When I write a problem statement that sounds specific, I want to check it for soft words and for success criteria that sit outside the sentence, so I can catch a problem that is still Ill-Defined before I try to solve it.

frameworks.name: Problem exploration framework (Problem/Opportunity, Larger System, Goal, Map Hierarchy)

jobs.text: When I start on a vague problem or opportunity, I want to place it in its larger system, state the goal and map the hierarchy, so I can see where the real problem sits before I narrow it.
When I have mapped the levels of a system, I want to ask how to improve its elements, their interactions, the whole and its purpose, so I can list innovation opportunities at each level.
When I start work on a problem, I want to place it as undefined, ill-defined, well-defined, or wicked by where I am in the search, so I can choose tools that fit this stage.
When I want an AI tool to do part of the work, I want to sort my problem by type first, so I can decide whether to automate with a check or keep the thinking in my own hands.
When I review my bank of ideas, I want to count how many are well-defined and how many are not, so I can see when the present is narrowing my thinking.

frameworks.name: Problem Typology Framework / The Taxonomy of Problems

jobs.text: When I start on a problem, I want to classify it as un-defined, ill-defined, or well-defined, so I can choose the right tools and timeline for it.
When I hold a problem that is still vague, I want to know which stage it is in, so I can refine it from un-defined to ill-defined to well-defined instead of jumping to a solution.
When I am about to run a design method on a problem, I want to name its type and give a verdict, so I can decide to run the method, hold and explore more, or switch tools.
When I choose which problem to work on, I want to test whether it is worth the effort, so I can avoid building on a weak problem.

frameworks.name: Problem-solving framework (What problem/opportunity, What about the larger system, What's your goal)

jobs.text: When I start on a problem or an opportunity, I want to name it, place it in the larger system and state my goal, so I can work on the right problem at the right level.

When I have an idea or a domain I care about, I want to work down from a vague question to a well-defined problem worth solving, so I can build my solution and business case on a problem that is real.
When I study a user's need, I want to map each step and rate it, so I can find the steps most worth improving.

When I have found a step that people rate high in importance and low in satisfaction, I want to ask what job they are really trying to get done at that step, so I can aim at the progress they seek and not only at the product they use.
When I lead a team that must innovate, I want people to feel safe to speak up and fail, so I can hear problems early.
When I see my team treat every failed attempt as a setback, I want to frame failure as the normal result of doing something new, so I can keep people willing to try.

frameworks.name: PWS Framework (Problem/Opportunity, Larger System, Goal, Map Hierarchy)

jobs.text: When I have an idea or a domain but no clear problem yet, I want to start from the problem instead of the solution, so I can find a problem worth solving before I build anything.
When I do not know which tools to reach for, I want to name whether my problem is un-defined, ill-defined or well-defined, so I can ask the questions and use the tools that fit that kind of problem.
When I have a solution I am excited about, I want to check that it also has a problem worth solving and a business case, so I can tell a real innovation from a gadget.
When I get ready to pitch my venture, I want to lead with one main problem and state my answer first, so I can make the listener care before I show the solution.
When I have drafted my pitch and it sounds good, I want to run it back through is it real, can we win and is it worth it, so I can turn a story into a pitch that holds up.
When I weigh an opportunity, I want to answer is it real, can we win, is it worth it, so I can decide to fund it or stop.
When I write my value proposition, I want to read the answers to real, win and worth together and look for the weakest one, so I can state the proposition only when all three hold.
When I have built my pitch and am about to face investors, I want to check it against real, win and worth, so I can answer their questions in whatever order they come.
When I am about to trust a forecast in a decision gate, I want to know how much each answer to real, win and worth depends on that forecast, so I can judge the gate on firm ground.
When I think I have an opportunity, I want to test whether it is real, whether we can win, and whether it is worth it, so I can commit only to problems that pass all three gates.
When I present my opportunity to a room of peers, investors or reviewers, I want to answer the three questions they are already asking, so I can win their trust before they find the gap themselves.
When I validate my solution or my business case, I want to let each answer send me back to rethink the problem, so I can keep the problem, solution and business case consistent.
When I sell to a business buyer with a budget, I want to say in one sentence how I grow their revenue and how I cut their costs, so I can show value in dollars and not in features.
When I am about to write my value proposition, I want to check that the problem is real, that I can win, and that it is worth it, so I can make the claim only when the weakest answer still holds.
When I validate my solution and then my business case, I want to go back and rethink the problem and the solution each time, so I can keep the whole value proposition true as I learn.

When I have a felt struggle but no clear problem yet, I want to name the job people are trying to get done and test whether it is a problem worth solving, so I can build my opportunities on a real need.
When I have found a job that no current product does well, I want to trace the lagging part of the system behind it, so I can tell whether I hold a well-defined problem or am still exploring.
When I see people buy the same product several times a day for different reasons, I want to name the purpose behind each purchase, so I can find the separate jobs that one product is hired for.
When I build scenarios of possible futures, I want to test each opportunity they show with the validation questions, so I can keep only the opportunities that hold up.

When I see my scenarios surface a handful of candidate opportunities, I want to deposit them in my bank of opportunities beside what my other tools found, so I can compare them before I choose which to validate.
When I have an idea I cannot judge on paper, I want to build a quick model of it, so I can learn from real tests before I commit money.

When I know my idea can work but not how it will feel to use, I want to build a prototype as the step between proof of concept and minimum viable product, so I can close that doubt before I test if anyone wants it.
When I must commit to an uncertain opportunity, I want to make small investments that keep my right to expand or stop later, so I can learn before I bet big.
When I see my company wave off an early technology that could end its core business, I want to fund it as a real option and protect it, so I can keep the right to grow it if it proves out.
When I feel a decision is wrong but cannot say why, I want to state my gut feeling openly without having to justify it, so I can put emotions on the table as data for the decision.

When I lead my team through a launch decision, I want each person's anxiety and pull heard as one reading among the facts and risks, so I can weigh feelings openly instead of letting the loudest one decide.
When my plan feels safe, I want to ask what would have to be true for my product to disappear, so I can find weak assumptions early.
When I have built a business case and someone is about to fund it, I want a red team to attack it on purpose, so I can find what is wrong before the check is written.
When I see my organization settle on one view of a threat, I want a standing group with the authority to argue the opposite, so I can stop consensus from passing for certainty.
When I have written an alternative to an industry belief and I like it too much, I want to hand it to someone whose job is to break it, so I can test my what-if before I commit to it.

frameworks.name: Resources Processes and Values / RPV Framework

jobs.text: When I ask whether an organization can pursue a new or disruptive opportunity, I want to check its resources, processes, and values, so I can see what it can and cannot do.
When a large incumbent is slow to answer a new threat, I want to check its resources, processes and values one by one, so I can find what really blocks it from responding.
When I review a past decision, I want to judge the reasoning and not only the result, so I can learn the right lesson.
When a system will not improve, I want to find the one lagging part that holds it back, so I can aim my effort there.
When a dominant design has locked but one part still lags behind the rest, I want to take that lagging part to reverse salient work, so I can find the next problem the locked design exposes.
When a system cannot fix its lagging part from inside the old design, I want to look for a new system that gets around it, so I can see where a whole new design may emerge.
When a system I study improves everywhere but one place, I want to find the one lagging part that holds the rest back, so I can aim my effort where a fix lets the whole system advance.

When a Jobs to Be Done study shows a step that matters a lot and is served badly, I want to trace it to the lagging part of the system behind it, so I can see where the technology sits on its S-curve and whether I hold a well-defined problem.

When my product life cycle map shows one stage that holds up every stage after it, I want to take that stage to reverse salient work, so I can open the problem at the bottleneck and not at a stage that only looks weak.

When the problems in a locked dominant design keep appearing one after another, I want to name the one component that holds the whole system back, so I can work on the next lagging part and not the parts that are already ahead.
When I weigh an opportunity in my bank, I want to score its risk as the cost of a first honest test in money, months and reputation, so I can stage the bet small enough to survive a no.
When I can find a statistic with a history behind what I do not know, I want to treat it as risk and insure, hedge, diversify or reduce it, so I can save exploration for what has no odds.
When a problem keeps coming back, I want to trace it down to its real cause, so I can fix the cause and not only the symptom.
When the fix for a customer need looks obvious, I want to keep asking why past the first fixable cause and then rank the causes I find, so I can choose the cause that is worth my effort.
When a technology I watch is improving less for each unit of effort, I want to place it on its S-curve, so I can tell if the top of the curve is an opening for a new problem worth solving.
When I manage a portfolio across three horizons, I want to place a Horizon 2 technology on its S-curve, so I can decide when it has earned its move into Horizon 1.
When a cheaper entrant attacks an incumbent, I want to check whether the incumbent's own S-curve is flattening, so I can tell a real disruption from a hope.

When I plan the demonstration of a dual-use technology, I want to check where it sits on its maturity curve at the moment the demonstration lands, so I can tell whether the demonstration will give me a lead or reset the whole field.
When I work in a complex situation where cause and effect are unclear, I want to run small experiments that are safe to fail, so I can watch what grows and learn without a big loss.
When I do not know which field holds the answer to my problem, I want to describe how my problem works at a deep, structural level, so I can find a twin in a distant field and borrow its solution.

When I see that something in nature already does what my product must do, I want to write the organism's chain from parts to action, so I can transfer the mechanism and not the organism into an engineered product.
When I have several candidate analogies from far fields, I want to write each one's chain and mark which links I know and which I guess, so I can see which analogy is worth testing first.

When the future of my domain is open and I am stuck in today's view, I want to build several plausible futures from the key uncertainties, so I can find problems and opportunities nobody is looking at yet.

When I must place a large, long-term bet and cannot predict which future will arrive, I want to test my strategy against several equally possible futures, so I can prepare for any of them instead of betting on one forecast.
When I need far-off bets to fill the long horizon of my portfolio, I want to build scenarios of possible futures, so I can stock that horizon with candidates worth exploring.
When I build scenarios of the future, I want to check that each one holds together by its own logic, so I can trust it enough to look for opportunities inside it.
When the future of my domain is too uncertain to predict, I want to build a few equally possible futures from key trends, so I can find opportunities I would miss by looking only at the present.
When one stage of a product life cycle is about to see its rules change, I want to build several possible futures for that stage, so I can see which problems the change could open.
When I have found the trigger that could break a dominant design, I want to test that trigger against more than one story of what happens next, so I can see the futures the collapse could open.

When a question about the future is too broad for anyone to answer directly, I want to build scenarios and pick one corner of them to work in, so I can turn the broad question into a set of opportunities I can explore.
When I build something new in an established industry, I want to expect that it will break part of the old order, so I can plan for the breakage and not be surprised by it.

When a new offer strikes at the foundations of existing firms and not only at their margins, I want to recognize it as a technological discontinuity, so I can see that the industry is about to be remade.
When I find an opportunity, I want to ask whether I am bringing something new that knocks down what stood before or spotting a gap that was already there, so I can choose how to act on it.

When I believe something about my customer or market, I want to state it as a falsifiable hypothesis and run the cheapest test that could prove it wrong, so I can let the data, not my conviction, decide.
When I want to challenge an industry belief, I want to state it as a claim that the data could prove wrong, so I can challenge it instead of only complaining about it.
When I have ranked the bottlenecks that hold a field back, I want to turn each one into a hypothesis I can refute, so I can drop a refuted bottleneck and move the next one up.
When I write my problem statement, I want it to say what I would see if it were false, so I can validate the problem with a pattern of evidence and not one interview.
When a field has a goal that people say is impossible, I want to map the bottlenecks that block progress and rank them, so I can fund and test the one that unlocks the most.
When my first version worked and I plan the next one, I want to resist adding every feature I held back, so I can avoid an overbuilt second system.
When my market looks stable, I want to watch for weak signals at its edges, so I can see a turning point coming before it hits me.
When I have to convince a prospect, I want my product to produce one real insight on their own live problem, so I can let them sell themselves instead of pitching.
When I have many texts about a domain, I want to map the concepts and how they link, so I can find hidden clusters and gaps between ideas.
When I lead a team on hard innovation work, I want to put the team's needs and growth first, so I can earn trust and get their best work without relying on authority.

When I want to think more creatively in my daily work, I want to practice Leonardo's habits of curiosity, learning from experience, sharp senses, comfort with ambiguity and seeing connections, so I can notice links that others miss.
When my organization keeps repeating the same mistakes, I want to check it for Senge's learning disabilities, so I can find what stops it from learning and adapting.
When my organization bets on a single forecast, I want to build a small set of distinct scenarios in the way Shell did, so I can prepare for a shock before it happens.
When leaders expect one future, I want to tell two contrasting and plausible stories from the same facts, so I can break their single view and prepare for both.
When I must open a document or talk on a hard problem, I want to state the situation, the complication, the question, and then my answer, so I can bring my audience to my main point fast.

When I come back from research with a pile of findings, I want to say what I now believe as one top-line answer earned by situation, complication and question, so I can tell people my conclusion and not my notes.
When my pitch beats are drafted, I want to run them back through the situation, complication, question and answer check, so I can make sure a skeptical investor can follow the argument.
When one way of leading works with some people and fails with others, I want to match my style to how ready each person is, so I can give each one the direction or freedom they need.
When a group argues in circles, I want everyone to wear the same hat at once, so I can examine the idea from each side in turn.
When my hypothesis is still fuzzy and I am about to put numbers on it, I want to look at it through each hat in turn, so I can sharpen it into a hypothesis worth the analysis that comes next.

frameworks.name: Social network theory of innovation opportunities

jobs.text: When I look for where new opportunities come from, I want to map my ties and find the weak ties and bridges to other groups, so I can reach the new information that shows an opportunity.
When people disagree about what the problem even is, I want to map the messy situation and each group's view of it, so I can agree on changes that are both wanted and possible.
When I explore an undefined problem space where nobody owns the question yet, I want to frame the messy situation as a system of views, so I can start the search with a map and not a guess.
When something in my system builds up or drains away over time, I want to map what accumulates and the rates that fill and empty it, so I can see why the problem keeps growing even after a fix.
When I need one complete picture of a system, I want to combine my causal loop map with stock and flow diagrams, so I can see both the factors involved and how they push on each other.

When I have drawn my system map and someone asks what we should actually do, I want to use my stocks and flows as the raw material for a leverage brief, so I can pick the change that will move the system.
When I see my venture face hard facts, I want to face them fully and still keep faith that I will succeed, so I can act on reality without losing heart.
When I plan beyond the next year or two, I want to explore several plausible futures instead of betting on one forecast, so I can prepare for change before it arrives.
When my industry shows a sudden shift in one force around it, I want to test whether it is a 10x change, so I can tell a real inflection point from normal noise before it is too late.
When I explore a domain for its next big problem, I want to look for where a dominant design could fall apart through a strategic inflection point, so I can find where the next opportunities open.
When a force is already moving in my domain, I want to follow its line forward in clear steps, so I can see what it will destroy and what problems it will open.
When I choose an axis for a scenario, I want to check whether a plain extrapolation would already have called it, so I can drop settled forces that only look uncertain.
When I must forecast and no single method is reliable, I want to average extrapolation with polls, models and expert judgment, so I can cut the error of my forecast.
When my pitch or idea does not stick with listeners, I want to make it simple, unexpected, concrete, credible, emotional, and told as a story, so I can make people remember and act on it.
When I build a small team for complex design work, I want one lead to own the core work with others in clear support roles, so I can keep the work fast and consistent.
When I call a new offer disruptive, I want to check where it started, who it served first and which way it moved, so I can tell a real disruption from a bigger sustaining improvement.

When I run an established business and a cheaper entrant starts where I am not looking, I want to choose on purpose to ignore it, strengthen my core, fight it or set up a separate unit, so I can respond before my mainstream customers switch.

When I plan how my own venture will enter against an incumbent, I want to read whether I am picking a head-on fight or starting from a foothold the incumbent ignores, so I can choose the fight I can actually win.
When the same problem keeps returning, I want to match it to a known system pattern, so I can find the real cause and the right point to act.

frameworks.name: Systematic approach to competitive innovation analysis

jobs.text: When I size up competitors in my market, I want to assess each one in the same structured way, so I can see where none of them is innovating.
When I need new product ideas, I want to apply templates such as subtraction and division to what I already have, so I can innovate inside my familiar world and not wait for a wild idea.
When I have found a leverage point in a system that no one controls, I want to help the people in it see the larger system and act on it together, so I can move the whole system and not just my part.
When a domain has many actors and links, I want to draw a map of its parts and connections, so I can see the system as a whole before I decide where to act.
When I am about to act on a systems map, I want to check every box and arrow on it first, so I can trust the map I act on.
When I see that the obvious lever is the one everyone reaches for, I want to check it against the systems map, so I can find the lever closer to the loop that drives the problem.
When a problem keeps coming back no matter which part I fix, I want to map the elements, links and purpose of the whole system, so I can find where the system itself has to change.
When I am about to add a fix to a system that seems to work, I want to trace each loop the fix sets off, so I can catch the unintended consequences before they cost more than the fix gains.
When I look for an innovation opportunity inside a complex social problem, I want to map the systems around it to find its leverage points, so I can find openings that simple problems no longer hold.

frameworks.name: Systems Thinking and Wicked Problems combined

jobs.text: When my problem is tangled with other problems and every fix changes the system, I want to map how the parts connect and push where the map shows a lever, so I can address the problem without making the system worse.
When my push on a system has worked, I want to ask what the system does back, so I can catch the side effects before they undo the gain.
When my map shows the lever but the people in the system will not pull it, I want to lead them through the change they must make, so I can turn the map into action.
When the market for my opportunity already exists and can be counted, I want to estimate the total, serviceable and obtainable market, so I can see how big the part I can really reach is.
When I want to push a field of science forward, I want to map its tech tree and find the bottlenecks that choke progress, so I can choose which obstacle is worth attacking first.
When I see several paths to a research goal, I want to tag the main limit on each path as physics or assumption, so I can tell hard limits from beliefs I could test.

When I work in a field that has followed one roadmap for years, I want to treat that roadmap as a hypothesis about where the bottleneck is, so I can notice when its central assumption runs into physical limits.
When people start to adopt my new technology, I want to know which group adopts now and which comes next, so I can change my approach before I fall into the gap between them.
When a solution already exists in another industry, I want to move it into the domain where the problem is open, so I can solve the problem with proven technology.
When I judge a new technology, I want to map who makes it, who uses it and what it means to them, so I can see opportunities and blockers the device alone hides.

When I carry a capability from one industry or place into another, I want to check the rules, approvals, habits and buyers that stay behind, so I can test whether it will work in the new place before I spend anything.
When my work is in progress and I cannot see its problems, I want candid feedback from peers who have no power over it, so I can improve it while I stay in charge.
When I set up project teams from different fields, I want them to give feedback on each other's work in progress, so I can combine their views into a better result.
When I am offered many options that all sound useful, I want to keep only those that fit my core purpose, so I can make decisions that stay true to why the venture exists.

frameworks.name: The Chasm Framework / Crossing the Chasm

jobs.text: When early adopters buy my product but mainstream buyers do not follow, I want to find the gap between those two groups, so I can change what I offer to win the mainstream.

When I plan how to reach the mainstream market, I want to pick one niche narrow enough to build the full whole product for and win outright, so I can turn that win into the peer story the next niche believes.
When I think I understand my idea, I want to explain it in plain words to someone outside my head, so I can find the parts that are not finished yet.

When I am about to build on a number or a cause someone told me, I want to check whether I could rebuild that claim myself from something more basic, so I can avoid resting my map on borrowed authority.
When I think I know why a pattern in my cases happens, I want to explain the cause simply enough that a stranger can say what would prove it wrong, so I can test the explanation before I build on it.

When my organization keeps repeating the same mistakes, I want to build personal mastery, mental models, shared vision, team learning and systems thinking, so I can turn it into an organization that learns.
When I am tempted to change direction after every setback, I want to keep pushing in one consistent direction, so I can build momentum that compounds over time.
When my pitch opens with what I built and people do not care, I want to start from why the work matters, then how, then what, so I can move people to act.
When I study a problem from the outside, I want to move from its what and its how down to its why, so I can understand why it hurts the people who live it.
When I decide to start a venture, I want to write down why I am starting it as a belief about what is broken, so I can open my later pitch with a hypothesis people can test.
When I keep reacting to one event after another, I want to dig below to the patterns, structures and beliefs that produce them, so I can act on the cause and not the symptom.
When I size up an idea, I want to separate what is uncertain from what is risky, so I can choose where to play and see where the idea is exposed.
When I must choose a few bets from my bank of opportunities, I want to compare them on how much uncertainty and how much risk each carries, so I can hold a deliberately mixed portfolio.
When I sort opportunities into now, new and next, I want to check which ones exploit high uncertainty while keeping risk low, so I can find the true next bets.
When I run a company that does well by serving its best customers, I want to see how a cheaper, simpler offer could grow from below, so I can act before good management makes me miss it.

When I start a new venture against strong incumbents, I want to compete in the emerging and disruptive space they tend to lose and not in their sustaining race, so I can avoid the fight their customers and resources let them win.
When I interview customers about my idea, I want to ask questions even a kind friend cannot answer with a polite lie, so I can learn what is true.

When I talk to one customer each week to find opportunities under the outcome I chose, I want to ask about one specific thing that happened to them recently and write it down as their own need, so I can grow my opportunity map from what is true in their life.
When I have a claim on my system map that came only from what people told me, I want to test it with questions about a real past event, so I can find the true bottleneck and not the polite one.
When I gather a group to generate ideas, I want to design the session with clear rules and a strong question, so I can get many good ideas and not a few safe ones.
When I must convince a skeptical reader, I want to put the answer first and group my support under it, so I can be followed and believed.
When my team has finished its research and reports what it found, I want to force one sentence of what we believe is true, so I can turn a pile of findings into an answer.
When I prepare a startup pitch on a business case that is already tested, I want to shape it answer first with grouped reasons, so I can make the true parts survive being said out loud.

frameworks.name: The Scenario Matrix Tool / 2x2 Scenario Matrix

jobs.text: When two important forces in my domain are truly unknowable, I want to cross them in a two-by-two grid of four futures, so I can find opportunities that hold up in each world.
When I start a scenario exercise for my domain, I want to list every force, trend and development shaping it, so I can pick the two that matter most for my grid.
When I notice scattered early signals at the edge of my field, I want to group them into patterns and test them as possible trends, so I can prepare before the trend becomes obvious to everyone.

When I suspect the dominant design in my field is starting to break, I want to watch for user complaints, fringe experiments and voices that say the status quo cannot last, so I can see the break before it is obvious.

When my organization must run today's business and build tomorrow's, I want to split the work into managing the present, letting go of the past and creating the future, so I can fund all three without one killing the others.
When I plan an intervention in a system, I want to lay out the causal path from my activities to the outcome and the assumption behind each step, so I can see which link I must test first.

When I work with stakeholders who disagree about which interventions will work, I want to draw each stakeholder's theory of change as an explicit causal map, so I can help them understand each other and check their assumptions.
When my running operation is late and losing money, I want to find the one station that limits the whole flow, so I can fix that first instead of everything at once.

frameworks.name: Theory of Jobs to Be Done

jobs.text: When I plan how my venture will win, I want to dominate a small market first and build proprietary technology, network effects, scale and brand, so I can grow from a base competitors cannot easily take.
When my business case is about to face hard questions, I want to run it through Thiel's seven questions one by one, so I can find the weak answer before a panel does.
When I must decide without knowing how things will turn out, I want to treat the choice as a bet with odds, so I can judge my decision by its quality and not only by its result.

When I need an insight to solve a problem, I want to choose between brute force, targeted development, and waiting for a eureka moment by the type of problem, so I can spend my effort on the approach that fits.

When I judge whether an idea can become an innovation, I want to check that it has a problem worth solving, a solution that works and a business case that lets it scale, so I can see which part is still missing.
When I start from an invention I already have, I want to look for the most important problem it could solve, so I can avoid settling for the first small problem I find.
When I have written my business case, I want to treat it as a promise that the solution can grow and test that promise at a larger scale, so I can learn how the real world responds before I spread.
When my portfolio mixes defending the core with new bets, I want to sort each opportunity into now, new, or next, so I can fund each horizon on purpose and not let the core eat the future.
When I worry about what could put my company out of business, I want to name the next opportunity that would do it, so I can build it before someone else does.

When I must judge how innovation will change an industry, I want to read the signals of change, the likely winner of each competitive battle and the strategic choices each firm makes, so I can predict where the industry goes from theory and not from guesswork.
When I assume today's way of doing things will last, I want to ask which signals of change I am ignoring, so I can see which future is coming before others do.

When my product does one job well and I plan how to grow it, I want to decide whether it should scale as a tool that finds more people with that job or as a platform that lets others do jobs I never planned, so I can choose the right way to scale.
When I design a business model, I want to check whether my offer needs two or more groups that need each other, so I can plan which side to bring in first.
When people cannot tell me what they would do with a flexible new device, I want to imagine the jobs they could find for it, so I can design a platform that no focus group would ask for.
When I teach a hard topic, I want to start from the big idea and move down level by level to the details, so I can help learners see how each part fits.
When I must build an argument for a document, I want to start from my main point and work down to the supporting points, so I can make the logic clear before I write.
When my team does only what is asked, I want to lead with a clear vision, challenge their thinking, and give each person attention, so I can help them do more than they expected.
When I have data on how a trend moved in the past, I want to project its line forward, so I can estimate where it will be and when it will matter.
When I build a fancier forecasting model, I want to check it against a plain projection of the trend, so I can trust the model only when it beats that line.
When I am about to project a trend, I want to write down the horizon, how noisy the data is and whether I have real data, so I can pick a method that fits the question.
When I study the future of a domain, I want to push one trend to its extreme, so I can see the problems and opportunities it would create for the whole system.

When I need to stock my opportunity bank with candidates for an undefined domain, I want to run one real trend to its absurd end and list what breaks, so I can deposit a handful of candidate problems that I can later turn into well-defined ones.
When I want more insights, I want to look for them along more than one path, not only by escaping a fixation, so I can find insights that a single path would miss.
When every option inside my current frame has failed, I want to reverse the assumption I have been holding fixed, so I can break out of the trap and reach an insight.
When I meet a fact that does not fit my model, I want to keep it and replace the belief it breaks, so I can reach an insight and not just patch my old story.
When I hold many ideas that seem unrelated, I want to look for two things that have never been joined, so I can reach an insight by connection.

When improving one part of my design makes another part worse, I want to name the contradiction and look up how other fields already got past it, so I can resolve it instead of settling for a tradeoff.
When I cannot see the flaws in my own decisions, I want a small group that agrees to test my reasoning honestly, so I can make better decisions than I would make alone.
When I review a decision with my group, I want us to take it apart before we know how it turned out, so I can judge the quality of the decision and not just the result.
When my new team starts to fight or stall, I want to see which stage of forming, storming, norming, or performing it is in, so I can lead it through that stage instead of treating it as failure.
When I face an unclear decision, I want to sort what I cannot know from the risks I can measure, so I can explore the first and manage the second.

When I choose which opportunities in my bank to pursue, I want to prefer the ones whose solution sits in the high uncertainty and low risk quadrant, so I can explore where others hesitate without betting what I cannot lose.
When I am not sure that my venture fits a startup at all, I want to place it on the uncertainty and risk grid, so I can see if I am really running an insurer, a moonshot or a settled market.
When I look for opportunities through the lens of needs, I want to find the gap between where a person is and the progress they seek, so I can see needs they cannot name themselves.
When I look for a problem worth solving in a new field, I want to log many first-hand needs before I judge any of them, so I can choose from a broad and honest list.
When I hold a long list of needs, I want to screen it step by step with clear criteria, so I can land on the few needs worth building against.
When I watch a user go through a process, I want to rate each step on importance and satisfaction, so I can find the steps that matter most and work worst today.

When I must decide whether a market is worth entering, I want to read each rated step against the four corners of importance and satisfaction, so I can tell the sweet spot from incumbent ground and over-served steps.

When I ask how AI could change what a user is trying to do, I want to go back to the steps of their process and rate them for importance and satisfaction, so I can see which steps a new tool would really change.
When I want to understand a user's whole experience, I want to map every step and how they feel at each one, so I can find the hidden pains and openings between the touchpoints.

When I want a breakthrough to come on its own, I want to work through the four steps of perceiving the problem, setting the stage, insight, and critical revision, so I can stop skipping steps that I will pay for later.
When I hold many tools and do not know which one to use, I want to match each tool to the Usher step it serves, so I can pick the tool my current step needs.

When I start an innovation project and feel the pull to jump to ideas, I want to put my effort on Usher's first step, perceiving the problem, so I can find the right problem for me and not just any problem worth solving.
When I have a new technology, I want to prove it step by step, from proof of concept to the next rungs, so I can answer one question at a time and not build an expensive way to fail slowly.

When I am not sure which kind of proof to build next, I want to name the one assumption that would kill the idea, whether it is a technical mechanism, a human experience or market demand, so I can choose between a proof of concept, a prototype and a minimum viable product.
When a market shifts, I want to see where value is moving, so I can place my venture on the side it is flowing to.
When I pitch an offer, I want one clear statement of why a customer should buy, so I can set it apart from alternatives.
When I sell to a business buyer with a budget, I want to say in one sentence how I grow their revenue and how I cut their costs, so I can make my case in dollars and not in features.
When I choose where to launch, I want to start in the narrowest market where my value proposition is most obviously compelling, so I can win there first and then ask how large it can grow.
When I design an offer, I want to match my pain relievers and gain creators to customer jobs, so I can build something customers want.
When I have a well-defined problem and must say what a solution has to deliver, I want to state the pains it must relieve and the gains it must create, so I can test solutions against clear criteria.
When I change or reverse the terms of competition in a market, I want to look for the pains and gains that new trade-offs create, so I can find new jobs to be done and niche uses.
When I have a product idea, I want to match it to the jobs, pains, and gains of a specific customer, so I can make a product that customers want.
When I look for new jobs to be done by changing my industry's terms of competition, I want to think in terms of pains and gains, so I can find trade-offs that point to jobs nobody serves.
When I have an insight that sounds right, I want to test it against stronger and stronger checks, so I can know it is real before I spend time on it.
When I want to rely on an answer an AI gave me, I want a check from outside the conversation that can disagree, so I can trust the claim for more than how plausible it sounds.
When I count a friend's agreement as evidence for my problem, I want to ask what happened, when and what could corroborate it, so I can tell sincere agreement from evidence of behavior.
When I take a new technology to market, I want to treat each stage as a step that earns the right to continue, so I can match people and money to what each stage needs.
When I write the business case report for my venture, I want to show how much uncertainty it removes, so I can buy the right to continue to the next stage.

frameworks.name: Wallas Four-Stage Model of the Creative Process

jobs.text: When my creative work is stuck, I want to know which stage I am in, from preparation to incubation, illumination, and verification, so I can give that stage what it needs instead of forcing an answer.

frameworks.name: Week 7 Combining Tools for Deep Opportunity Exploration

jobs.text: When one tool has shown me a gap but not an opportunity, I want to hand that diagnosis to a second tool, so I can turn the gap into an opportunity I can act on.
When my ideas come by accident from things I happen to see or feel, I want to run them through a planned chain of tools, so I can replace random ideas with structured discovery.
When I build a bank of opportunities in one domain, I want to run several different exploration tools on it, so I can collect candidates that no single lens would show.
When I have chosen an opportunity but my problem statement is still vague, I want to turn it into a bounded, falsifiable statement, so I can test whether a solution really meets it.
When I choose which few opportunities to advance from my bank, I want to write each one as a problem statement a stranger could test, so I can defend each pick over the ones I leave behind.
When I have found the few causes that matter most, I want to restate my problem around those causes and what a solution must deliver, so I can test it with the people who live with it.
When I decide how to use AI on a problem, I want to check whether my statement already holds its solution criteria, so I can use the AI on a clear target and not let it wander.

When I see my team argue positions, I want everyone to put the known facts and the missing facts on the table first and cite a source for each claim, so I can separate what we know from what we believe.
When I must choose between launching now, delaying or pivoting, I want to surface the real numbers before anyone argues, so I can base the call on facts and not on moods.
When a market looks crowded, I want to map what is served and what is not, so I can find the gaps no one fills yet.
When I find an empty spot on a white space map, I want to ask why it is empty before I call it a market, so I can avoid a gap that is empty for a good reason.
When mainstream buyers like my product but do not buy, I want to add every complement they need to feel safe in their own context, so I can sell beyond the early adopters.

When I set the gate before I scale to cautious buyers, I want to check that I have the whole product for one segment, including support, setup and the tools it must work with, so I can scale only when a buyer from that segment would vouch for it to a peer.
When I face a vague situation, I want to move from asking why, to imagining what if, to working out how, so I can turn a shapeless doubt into a problem I can act on.
When I have taken a first step and the world has responded, I want to turn that response into a new Why, so I can keep the questioning running instead of treating the work as done.

When I work through one of the four lenses, an orthodoxy, a trend, an underused resource or an unnamed need, I want to run Why, What If and How on it, so I can turn what that lens shows me into a reframed problem.
When a problem resists every fix and keeps moving, I want to test whether it is wicked and map its system, so I can find the leverage points where an innovation can make a difference.
When I plan to run design thinking and the user looks like a symptom of a larger loop, I want to check if I am at the wicked edge, so I can map the system before I empathize with one user.
When I want to hand a problem to an AI tool, I want to check whether the people affected disagree about what the problem is, so I can keep the decision with them when it is wicked.
When I sort a new situation and nobody can say where the problem starts and stops, I want to treat it as wicked, so I can map it instead of trying to solve it.

When the people affected cannot agree on what my problem is and every fix I try changes it, I want to treat it as a wicked problem that I address and do not solve, so I can stop looking for one fix and work the tensions with the people involved.
When a wicked problem is too tangled to attack, I want to break it into bounded parts, so I can find one part I can define well enough to solve.

When I want to use AI on a problem the people involved disagree about, I want to treat the AI output as one input to a decision I make with them, so I can avoid letting a machine settle a dispute about values.
When the person I design for is a symptom of a tangle of loops, I want to map the system before I start design thinking, so I can see the loop that empathy with one user will not show.
When my organization has lost touch with the people it serves, I want to build real empathy for them across the whole company, so I can see needs that reports and data miss.
When a team argues over an idea, I want to state its real upside and the evidence behind it, so I can weigh the value honestly and not mistake cheerleading for a case.
When I face a high-stakes go or no-go call, I want someone to count honestly what each option is worth, delay included, so I can see the value that fear or momentum would hide.
